_comment: Presentation. ALL of it is TUNABLE and none of it is a mechanic. The expected feedback is 'too dark', 'the grass is the wrong green', 'the creatures don't move enough' — every one of those has to be answerable by editing this file rather than by editing a scene.
_comment_scale: Nothing here sets a collider or a hit range. Art is fitted to the gameplay size the species and the controller already declare; if a value in this file could change how far an attack reaches, it is in the wrong file.

trainer._comment_height: Metres, matched to the CharacterBody3D capsule in scenes/player/player.tscn. The model is measured and scaled to this, so a replacement of any size drops in without touching the scene.
trainer._comment_yaw: Degrees of correction for which way the source model faces. Verified from a survey frame, not assumed — there is no convention across asset packs.
trainer._comment_clips: Five clips, authored by tools/art_pipeline/blender/animate_humanoid.py and baked into the .glb, so the role and the clip name are the same string and nothing is retargeted. MQ1A rebuilt them as key-pose authored cycles (contact/loading/mid-stance/toe-off/whip/mid-swing/reach through a cyclic spline, on render-verified bone axes) with pelvis rotation, chest counter-rotation and head stabilisation.
trainer._comment_gait_speeds: OF5, TUNABLE. Metres per second each gait clip was AUTHORED for — animate_humanoid.py derives the cycle length and stride from these so a planted foot sweeps back under the body at the same speed the controller drives it. trainer_model.gd scales playback by actual ground speed / this value (clamped 0.5-1.4x in character_model.gd), so cadence stays honest through acceleration, slopes and any movement.json retune. If locomotion speeds are retuned by more than the clamp covers, re-bake the clips against the new numbers rather than widening the clamp: past ~1.4x a gait reads as frantic, not fast.
trainer._comment_libraries: Empty now, and kept as a key because the merge path still works. KayKit's Ranger needed it: that character ships a rig with zero clips and the motion in shared libraries. This model carries its own clips. Its skeleton is also NOT KayKit's — KayKit's character is about two heads tall and sheet 04's trainer is 6.25, so neither the weights nor the clips transfer between them.
trainer._comment_model: Sheet 04's trainer, produced through tools/art_pipeline. The body and the head were generated separately and grafted: nine whole-figure candidates across three rounds all came back with a blank ovoid for a face, because at a 30k budget spread over a standing figure an eye socket is smaller than the triangles available to describe it.

sky._comment: Mid-morning, high summer, clear. Taken from the key art board rather than invented: a warm low-contrast sky over saturated grass is most of what makes the reference read as inviting rather than as a tech demo.
sky._comment_panorama: An HDRI panorama, when the time of day names one. The procedural gradient below is the FALLBACK and stays because a missing texture should degrade to the old sky rather than to a black void. The critic measured the procedural sky's horizontal variation at 0.020 against Palworld's 0.140-0.289 and said the build sky 'contributes nothing' — a ProceduralSkyMaterial can make a vertical gradient and a soft sun blob and nothing else, ever. No amount of tuning puts a cloud in it.
sky._comment_panorama_ev8: EV8. day.hdr named here was pulled: a static equirect photo has its OWN baked-in sun position, unrelated to this file's sun.pitch_deg/yaw_deg, so whichever way a viewpoint faces, the photographed sky and the actual DirectionalLight3D can disagree about where the light is coming from. That is exactly what a blind pass caught -- one viewpoint's sky read as dusk while its own ground lit as bright midday, in the same frame, both driven by the same 'day' preset. The procedural gradient has no such seam: its glow is generated from the real sun direction, so it agrees with the ground in every direction, not just the survey's five. Costs the cloud detail the panorama bought; buys back the 'one sky/fog treatment shared everywhere' EV8 exists to deliver. TUNABLE -- naming a panorama here is legitimate again once one exists whose baked sun can be kept in sync, or once multiple panoramas are matched to sun position by heading.

sun._comment: One directional light. `pitch` well above the horizon so shadows are short and readable under a top-down-ish combat camera; long raking shadows look dramatic in a screenshot and hide the opponent in a fight.
sun._comment_shadow: Normal bias fights the acne that a heightmap terrain produces at grazing angles. Raise it if the ground looks striped; lower it if small props stop casting.
sun._comment_energy: Bright. The first pass at real lighting overshot into gloom: the arena went near-black and the creatures stopped being readable, which is a worse failure than the flat lighting it replaced. Value RANGE was the goal — bright sun, real shadows — not darkness.
sun._comment_pitch_r9_4: R9.4. Was -52. The blind critic found frames 01-04 'effectively flat-lit' -- boosting contrast 3x revealed almost no terrain form -- while frame 05, the only low-sun frame, was 'by a wide margin the best-lit frame in the set' and the only one whose value statistics land inside the references' range. Dropped to -44 rather than to 05's -13: the original comment's reason for a high sun is real (long raking shadows hide the opponent under a top-down-ish combat camera) and this keeps shadows short while giving slopes a lit and a shaded side. TUNABLE, and the thing to re-check first if combat readability regresses.

environment._comment: Tonemap and fog. ACES holds highlights on sunlit grass instead of clipping them to white, which was the single worst thing about the previous prototype's look.
environment._comment_exposure_ev4_lighting: EV4-textures-lighting. Was 1.22. Three blind-critic rounds on EV4-textures's own path frames independently named a blown-white sunlit path and (separately) an unmotivated dark diagonal band, and it took both diag_shadow_band.gd and diag_slope_check.gd (scratch, not shipped) to separate two different causes hiding under one description. `square-convergence`'s band IS a real occlusion shadow -- confirmed by toggling sun.shadow_enabled off, which removed it -- from the Barn 6m from that viewpoint's camera; raising directional_shadow/size back to 4096 changed nothing (pixel-identical edge), which rules out SA1's atlas cut as the cause. `grandpas-house-route`'s flanking bands are NOT a shadow at all -- identical with shadow_enabled true or false, identical with SSAO on or off, and the ground there measures dead flat (slope_degrees_at = 0.0 across the whole sampled width, confirmed with the heightfield's own function, no scene load needed). That one is pure contrast: ordinary grass at luma ~70-100 sitting next to a path blown to ~190-200 reads as 'a shadow with no caster' even though the grass itself is unremarkable. Fixing the blown highlight therefore addresses both: `near_luma` (tools/frame_stats.py, mean luma of the bottom 15% of frame) measured 0.692 on grandpas-house-route against Palworld's own 0.492-0.600, and the sunlit path itself sampled at ~197/255. A modest exposure trim did almost nothing (1.22 -> 0.95 moved the path 0/255 -- ACES's shoulder is that flat up here); it took a real cut to 0.6 to bring the path to ~151/255, inside the Palworld range. TUNABLE, and the first thing to revisit if 'day' reads dim elsewhere.
environment._comment_ambient_ev4_lighting: EV4-textures-lighting. Was 1.02. The Barn's real shadow measured near-black (luma 10-20/255) at its darkest, well under any reference near-field value -- lifting ambient is the one lever that reaches it without touching the sunlit path much (measured: tripling ambient moved the sunlit path only ~197->215, but moved the shadow floor ~15->40, because ambient is a much larger fraction of what a SHADOWED point receives). Went with a smaller, safer step than that -- 1.02 -> 1.5, not 3x -- because a big ambient increase measurably crept back into the sunlit path too once combined with the exposure cut above (both scale the same HDR value before tonemap), which would have undone the highlight fix. Left the shadow darker than ideal rather than fight that tradeoff further; see the EV4-textures-lighting DONE.md entry for what a blind pass said after this.
environment._comment_fog: Very light, and warm rather than grey. It exists to separate near hills from far ones; at any strength where you notice it as fog, it is too strong.
environment._comment_fog_measured: Halved from 0.0022. At the old density the blind critic measured `03-rise-overlook` at mean saturation 0.235 against 0.51 for a frame in the same biome, and said fog was 'eating the world rather than describing depth' — every object past ~150m a grey stamp. The reference does the same job with comparable haze and keeps a saturated tree band in front of it, so the fix is less fog, not less distance.
environment._comment_fog_colour_ev8: EV8. Was #cdd0c6, which does not match sky.horizon_colour (#b9c8cf) above. fog_sky_affect is 0 on purpose (see below), so the sky is never fogged -- which means the fog colour and the horizon colour are the ONLY two things that have to agree for terrain fading into the distance to meet the sky without a seam. A blind pass caught the mismatch as a hard pale band sitting in the middle of a frame, well short of the true horizon: distant terrain fogs to #cdd0c6 while the sky right above it sits at #b9c8cf, and the two visibly disagree. Matched to horizon_colour exactly.
environment._comment_ambient: Sky ambient with a real colour underneath it. `sky_contribution` blends between the two. Quadrupling ambient energy with pure sky ambient moved the survey frames by NOTHING — sky radiance does not reach the terrain under the Compatibility renderer the harness is forced to use — while an explicit colour lifted the shaded ground by 55%. Specifying both means shaded ground is filled under either renderer, and 'shadows are filled by this much of this colour' is a decision somebody made rather than a side effect of a procedural sky.
environment._comment_ambient_r9_4: R9.4. Was 1.25. High ambient is what removed the bottom of the value range: the critic measured the 5th-percentile luminance of frames 01 and 03 at 126 and 117 -- the DARKEST 5% of those images was still a mid-tone -- against 17 for palworld-04, and luminance standard deviation at 28-36 against the references' 52-69. Ambient light with nowhere to fall off is a flat frame by construction. Cut to 0.95, not lower: this file already records one pass that overshot into gloom and made the arena unreadable, and the ground albedo itself now carries most of the value drop (see terrain_playground's grass tint). TUNABLE.
environment._comment_fog_r9_4: R9.4. Halved again, 0.0011 -> 0.00055, and the colour warmed off neutral grey. The critic: 'fog is eating the world, not describing it' -- everything past the mid-ground washing to one pale value with no separation between hills, against palworld-04 which keeps three readable value planes at distance. It also produced the survey's most-reported inconsistency: frames 03 and 04 appear to have a flat cream sky, which is not sky at all but fogged-out terrain filling the upper frame, so two viewpoints of the same place look like different biomes. Less fog, not less distance. TUNABLE.
environment._comment_exposure_r9_4: R9.4 round 2. Was 1.05. Round 1 dropped the ground albedo (grass tint) AND cut ambient 1.25 -> 0.95 at the same time, and the two stacked: near-field luminance went 0.526 -> 0.271 and the open meadow read murky rather than merely un-blown-out. Exposure is the right knob to give it back, because it scales everything uniformly and so costs none of the desaturation the tint bought -- unlike raising ambient again, which would re-flatten the shadows that were the point. TUNABLE.

_comment_times: Named hours. Each states ONLY what it changes; everything else comes from the blocks above. `hour` (0-24) is when scripts/world/day_cycle.gd treats this as the active preset -- see R5.1.
_comment_times_why: The previous survey shipped a frame called `05-spawn-low-sun` whose sky was BIT-IDENTICAL to the midday frame beside it — 46.8% of the image pixel-for-pixel the same — because dropping the sun meant rotating a DirectionalLight3D and nothing else. The sun disc, sky gradient, horizon haze and fog all stayed at noon. The key art board asks for 'day and night create different moods'; a sky that does not move with the sun cannot give one. So the hour is one value and everything derives from it. Nothing should reach for the Sun node directly again.
_comment_day_cycle: TUNABLE (CLAUDE.md 'Tunable Values'): how fast the clock runs and when the world counts as genuinely dark, for scripts/world/day_cycle.gd. No gameplay reads these yet -- R5.1 is presentation only, matching GAME_DESIGN.md 24's 'do not just add levels to every creature at night'; nocturnal spawn rules are a later, separate decision.

day._comment: Mid-morning, high summer, clear. The default, and what the biome is designed around.

golden._comment: Late afternoon. Long shadows, warm key, the sky's blue pushed down and the horizon lifted to amber. This is the mood the key art's own sunset panel is selling, and it is the one hour where the meadow gets its warm end of the palette for free.

sky._comment_energy_ev8_retired: EV8 tried scaling golden.hdr's energy down twice (1.0 -> 0.6 -> 0.35) to fix a blown-white horizon, and even 0.35 still blew out roughly two-thirds of the frame. Retired along with the panorama below rather than pushed further -- same root cause as day.hdr: a static photo's own baked sun position does not track sun.pitch_deg/yaw_deg, so nothing here can make its glare agree with wherever this preset's actual low sun is pointed.
sky._comment_panorama_ev8: EV8. Dropped golden.hdr, same reasoning as the base sky block above -- a static panorama's own baked sun cannot track this preset's actual sun.pitch_deg/yaw_deg, and here that showed up as blown-white glare rather than a mismatched hue. The procedural gradient's sun glow is generated from the real light direction, so at a low golden-hour angle it puts the glow where the sun actually is and holds highlights the way ACES is tuned to.

environment._comment_fog_colour_ev8: EV8. Matched to horizon_colour (#e8b784) above, same reasoning as the day preset -- fog_sky_affect is 0, so fog colour and horizon colour are what has to agree for distant terrain to fade into the sky without a seam.
environment._comment_ambient_ev8: EV8. Was 1.15. A blind pass on the low-sun frame called the ground 'crushed almost to black' against a still-saturated sky -- the shadow side was losing terrain form entirely rather than reading as evening mood. TUNABLE -- the cool tint stays deliberately (real golden-hour fill from open sky reads cool against a warm key), only the amount lifted.

night._comment: No panorama exists for this yet (only day.hdr/golden.hdr were generated), so it falls back to the procedural gradient on purpose -- a missing texture degrading to the old sky beats a black void. The sun stands in for moonlight: low energy, cool, low in the sky rather than below the horizon so there is still one soft shadow direction to read.

sky._comment_panorama: Explicitly empty. The base `sky` block above names day.hdr; _merged() layers this dict on top of that one, so without this the night preset would silently inherit the DAY panorama instead of falling back to the procedural gradient.

environment._comment_fog_colour_ev8: EV8. Matched to horizon_colour (#1c2740) above, same reasoning as the day and golden presets.

_comment_creature_motion_removed: The procedural bob that used to be configured here is gone. The creatures are rigged and animated now, so they have real idle, walk, run, attack and death clips — faking motion on top of that would fight the animation.

villager_farmer._comment: R7.2, moved off Grandpa's rig by NP5 (owner directive 2026-08-12: the village should stop reading as clones of Grandpa and the trainer). Now NP4-rig's villager_female base -- a real second body, not a tint of the hero rig.
villager_farmer._comment_hair: NP7: villager_female_lod0.glb now ships a real separated `hair_ponytail` mesh (cut from the fused source, patched, re-skinned to Head in Blender) instead of the old single fused surface. `visible: true` here is the default look, unchanged from before this split -- but it now runs through character_model.gd's real find/toggle path (_apply_hair), not just a baked-in mesh nobody can hide. Present on all three villager_female-based configs (farmer, smith, ranger) so the base's default appearance is unaffected by the split.
villager_farmer._comment_tint_removed: Owner playtest report, second round, said this plainly: 'all of the NPCs still look like different hues across their whole body. it looks stupid.' The hair-only fix (NP-hair-colour, kept below) was the right MECHANISM but left `tint` still multiplying every surface on a rig that has exactly one material for skin, face AND clothes together (NP1-geometry's own documented limit) -- so a warm orange tint here was never just 'rustier wardrobe colour', it was an orange-tinted FACE, which is what actually reads as broken. `tint` removed outright (`#ffffff` is this codebase's own established identity multiply, confirmed by NP1's comment on `_shared_variant_material`: a white tint 'renders identically to before' the source art). The rig now shows its own as-authored colours, unmultiplied, and hair alone carries the differentiation -- which is what CLAUDE.md and spec 21 actually ask for.

hair._comment_color: Owner playtest report: NPCs should differ primarily by hair colour, not a whole-body hue shift (spec §21). villager_female's real hair_ponytail mesh (NP7) is the one part of this rig `tint` does NOT also multiply, so it is the actual per-material differentiator spec §21 asks for. Warm chestnut, distinct from smith's and ranger's below.

villager_keeper._comment: R7.2, moved off the trainer's rig by NP5 (owner directive 2026-08-12). Now NP4-rig's villager_male base, not the same body the player controls.
villager_keeper._comment_tint_removed: Owner playtest report, second round: NPCs still read as different hues across the whole body, 'looks stupid'. villager_keeper._comment_accessory_tried_and_reverted: A per-material belt-pouch accessory (its own mesh/material, distinct from the shared body/face one) was tried here as Oskar's differentiator from Callum (villager_quarryman) -- villager_male has no separable hair mesh (NP7 only cut one for villager_female), and CLAUDE.md's own fallback for that case is 'identical NPCs are preferable to ugly whole-model hue shifts', which reads as license to try a THIRD option first if one exists cheaply. It did not render correctly: `_attach_part`'s `Hips`-bone attachment (character_model.gd) placed and sized the pouch wrong in a real render -- a large box floating at chest height, not a small one at the hip -- for a reason not root-caused in this pass (the bone name and the giant-player scale-compensation path both checked out fine in isolation). Reverted rather than shipped broken: CLAUDE.md's own fallback applies exactly as written now that the cheap option failed a real visual check. Oskar and Callum are visually identical until a real per-material asset (or a correctly-positioned accessory) exists.

villager_smith._comment: R7.2, moved off the trainer's rig by NP5 (owner directive 2026-08-12). Now NP4-rig's villager_female base, same as villager_farmer's -- the two share a body but keep their own distinct tints, the way villager_keeper and villager_ranger already shared the trainer's rig before this item. NP6: the original #3f5a8c (value 0.55, luminance 0.35) read as a flat black silhouette in outdoor sun once NP2's fix made emission correctly reflect the tint -- both albedo AND the self-lit emission pass darken together now, and a source texture with mid/dark regions multiplied by this tint crushed to near-black. A first fix at the same saturation, value 0.72 (luminance 0.45), still rendered as an unlit silhouette in a real frame (round 1 of this item's blind pass) -- blue is the lowest-weighted channel in perceived luminance (Rec709 ~7%), so a saturated blue needs a much higher raw value than an equal-luminance warm tint before it stops reading dark, and a warm sun contributes little light back onto a blue-heavy albedo. Desaturated (0.55 -> 0.35) and brightened further (value 0.72 -> 0.88, luminance 0.67, matching villager_ranger's) genuinely stopped it reading as a black silhouette (round 2's blind pass), but it was still the visibly weakest of the cast -- the critic traced it to the face specifically, reading as 'pale grey-white... closer to unlit clay than skin'. Root cause: this rig has one fused mesh and one material (no separate skin surface -- the same limitation `NP1-geometry` documents for every human rig), so `tint` multiplies the face too, and a still-saturated blue (0.35) fights a warm skin albedo in a way farmer's orange or ranger's tan never do, because a cool hue has almost nothing in common with skin's high-red, low-blue channel balance. Desaturated further (0.35 -> 0.18) at the same high value so the multiply stops fighting the skin tone while the hue still reads as a pale chambray/steel-blue distinct from the cast's warmer colours.
villager_smith._comment_tint_removed: Owner playtest report, second round, overrides the caution in the comment above: the pale-blue tint this whole thread of comments fought three rounds to keep from reading as an 'unlit clay' face was STILL a tint on the face, and the owner's plain reaction ('looks stupid') means partial success is not the bar. Removed outright, same reasoning as farmer/keeper/ranger elsewhere in this file -- `#ffffff` never darkens or hues anything, so the specific failure mode this rig's history is all about (a saturated multiply crushing a dark source region toward black) cannot recur. Hair alone differentiates smith now.
